title: Eosinophilic Granuloma Complex

content_blocks.text: Cats—also called feline eosinophilic skin disease; term used for three distinct syndromes: eosinophilic plaque, eosinophilic granuloma, and indolent ulcer; grouped primarily according to their clinical similarities, their frequent concurrent (and recurrent) develop ment, and their positive response to corticosteroids; reaction pattern and not a final
Dogs— eosinophilic granuloma in dogs (EGD) rare; specific differences from cats listed separately.

Eosinophil—major infiltrative cell for eosinophilic granuloma and eosinophilic plaque, but not typically with indolent ulcer; most often associated with allergic or parasitic conditions but has a more general role in
Eosinophilic granuloma complex (EGC)—most often in cats with hypersensitivities to inhaled allergens, food, or insects, but can also be idiopathic with
EGD—may have both a genetic predisposition and a hyper sensitivity cause (especially in non-genetically susceptible breeds).

Related individuals with disease development in a colony of specific pathogen-free cats indicate that genetic predisposition (possible inheritable dysfunction of eosinophilic regulation) may be significant component for development.
Seasonal incidence in some geographic locations—insect or environmental allergen exposure.
